concepts.title: Microeconomics versus Macroeconomics
concepts.definition: Micro analysis studies single decision makers chasing private gain, while macro analysis treats the whole national economy as its unit and worries about prices, jobs and output taken together.
concepts.key_idea: Micro zooms into individual buyers and sellers; macro zooms out to economy-wide totals and policy.
question_patterns: which branch of economics treats the entire national economy as its unit and tracks economy-wide totals
why are inflation and unemployment macro issues rather than micro issues
explain how macroeconomics goes beyond individual buyers and sellers to cover policy goals of the state
state the main difference between individual agent analysis and aggregate analysis
compare what microeconomics and macroeconomics each try to explain
how does studying one market differ from studying all markets together

solution_steps.action: Identify the unit of study in each branch
solution_steps.explain: Micro takes one consumer, firm or market; macro takes the national economy as a single unit.
Micro agents maximise private profit or satisfaction, while macro policy pursues social goals such as jobs, stable prices and growth.
Any question about economy-wide totals, general prices or overall employment belongs to macro; questions about one buyer, seller or market belong to micro.

concepts.title: Aggregates and the Representative Good Simplification
concepts.definition: Because outputs, prices and jobs across sectors usually move together, macro analysis compresses the many goods of an economy into one imaginary representative commodity so that economy-wide behaviour can be tracked with few variables.
concepts.key_idea: Aggregates work because individual outputs, prices and employment tend to rise and fall together.
question_patterns: why can economists study a single representative commodity instead of every good
what makes aggregate analysis of an economy valid
explain the simplification used to analyse total production and employment
when does behaviour of one commodity mirror the behaviour of all commodities
how do output, price and employment levels of different goods move relative to each other
justify using one imaginary good to represent the entire economy

solution_steps.action: Note the co-movement of sector variables
solution_steps.explain: Food, industrial goods and services generally expand or contract together, as do their prices and jobs.
Pick one imaginary commodity whose production, price and employment stand for the economy-wide averages.

solution_steps.action: State the limitation of the shortcut
solution_steps.explain: Distinct traits of individual goods or sectors (say agriculture versus industry) are lost, so sometimes a few sector groups are kept instead of one.

concepts.title: Economic Agents and Decision Making
concepts.definition: Any individual or institution that takes decisions affecting the use of scarce resources - consumers choosing purchases, firms choosing output, governments, banks and corporations setting spending, taxes or interest - is an economic agent.
concepts.key_idea: Households, firms, banks and the state all act as decision-taking units in the economy.
question_patterns: who are called economic agents in an economy
name the decision-taking units that economists study
give examples of institutions that make economic decisions
what kinds of choices does an economic agent make
explain the term used for individuals and institutions taking economic decisions
how do households, firms and government each act as economic units

solution_steps.explain: An agent is any unit whose choices allocate resources - what to buy, produce, spend, tax or charge.
Consumers, producers, and bodies such as government, corporations and banks all qualify.

solution_steps.action: Match the example to the category
solution_steps.explain: A family buying food is a consumer agent; a company setting output is a producer agent; a central bank fixing rates is an institutional agent.

concepts.title: Emergence of Macroeconomics and Keynes
concepts.definition: Macroeconomics separated from classical thinking after John Maynard Keynes published his 1936 work arguing that an economy can stay stuck with lasting unemployment, an insight forced by the mass job losses and idle factories of the Great Depression that began in 1929.
concepts.key_idea: The Great Depression showed self-adjusting full employment to be false, and Keynes's 1936 general theory founded macroeconomics.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec101.txt, section 1.1 Emergence of Macroeconomics, page 5
question_patterns: when and how did macroeconomics emerge as a separate subject
which book and author are credited with founding macroeconomics
what role did the Great Depression play in the birth of macroeconomics
explain how Keynes challenged the classical full employment belief
why did economists start studying the economy as a whole in the 1930s
describe the failure of classical thinking during the 1929 depression

solution_steps.explain: Before Keynes, the dominant classical view held that all willing workers find jobs and factories run at capacity.
After 1929 output and jobs collapsed across Europe and North America; in the USA unemployment climbed from 3 percent to 25 percent between 1929 and 1933 while output fell about a third.
Keynes's 1936 General Theory examined the economy in its entirety and the interdependence of sectors, so macroeconomics was born.

concepts.title: Unemployment Rate
concepts.definition: The unemployment rate measures the share of the labour force that is without work yet actively seeking jobs; the labour force counts everyone either working or looking for work.
concepts.key_idea: Only jobless people who are searching count as unemployed; the denominator is the labour force, not the whole population.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec101.txt, section 1.1, unemployment rate definition, page 5
question_patterns: calculate the unemployment rate when jobless seekers and employed workers are given
find the percentage of the labour force that is unemployed
how is the unemployment rate of a country computed
work out the share of workers without jobs from labour force data
if 25 people are jobless and 75 are employed, what is the unemployment rate
define and compute the rate of unemployment from given numbers

solution_steps.action: Add employed and jobless seekers to get the labour force
solution_steps.explain: Everyone working plus everyone looking for work forms the labour force denominator.

solution_steps.action: Express jobless seekers as a percentage of the labour force
solution_steps.explain: Dividing seekers by the labour force and scaling by 100 gives the unemployment rate.

concepts.title: Features of a Capitalist Economy
concepts.definition: A capitalist economy is one where most production units are privately owned, output is made for market sale, and labour itself is hired and paid a wage rate rather than supplied by family members.
concepts.key_idea: Private ownership, market sale of output and wage-based hiring together mark an economy as capitalist.
question_patterns: what are the important features of a capitalist economy
state the characteristics that define a capitalist country
how does wage labour distinguish capitalist production from family production
explain private ownership of means of production in capitalism
why is production for sale in the market a capitalist trait
list the conditions under which an economy qualifies as capitalist

solution_steps.action: Check who owns the means of production
solution_steps.explain: In capitalism, capital, land and firms rest in private hands, unlike tribal or peasant settings.
Goods are made to be sold in the market for profit, not mainly for the producer's own use.
Workers sell their labour services for a wage, which separates them from family-based farm labour.

concepts.title: Factors of Production and Factor Payments
concepts.definition: A capitalist firm combines land, capital and labour under an entrepreneur; each factor earns a payment from sales revenue - land receives rent, capital receives interest, labour receives wages, and whatever remains is the entrepreneur's profit.
concepts.key_idea: Revenue is split among factor payments, and profit is the residual left after paying land, capital and labour.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec101.txt, section 1.2, revenue split into rent, interest, wages, profit, page 6
question_patterns: how is a firm's revenue divided among the factors of production
calculate the entrepreneur's profit from revenue and factor payments
which payment does each factor of production earn in a capitalist firm
find the residual income left for the entrepreneur after paying rent interest and wages
name the reward earned by land labour and capital respectively
given sales revenue and factor payments, work out profit

solution_steps.action: Add up the contracted factor payments
solution_steps.explain: Rent for land, interest for capital and wages for labour are owed before profit is counted.

solution_steps.action: Subtract factor payments from sales revenue
solution_steps.explain: Whatever revenue remains after the three contracted payments is the entrepreneur's profit.

concepts.title: Investment Expenditure
concepts.definition: Spending that raises the economy's productive capacity - buying new machinery or erecting new factories, often financed out of profits kept back by producers - is investment expenditure.
concepts.key_idea: Investment means capacity-building purchases, not purchases of consumer goods.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec101.txt, section 1.2, investment expenditure paragraph, page 6
question_patterns: what is meant by investment expenditure in macroeconomics
which spending by producers counts as investment
why is buying new machinery called investment
distinguish investment spending from consumption spending
how do retained profits become new plant and machinery
explain the term used for expenses that raise productive capacity

solution_steps.explain: Only outlays that add to future production - machines, buildings - are investment.
Producers often channel past profits into such purchases, expanding output next period.
Payments for raw materials used up or for consumer goods do not build capacity and are not investment expenditure.

concepts.title: Four Sectors of the Economy
concepts.definition: Macroeconomics pictures the economy as four interacting sectors - households that consume, save and pay taxes; firms that produce; the government that makes laws, taxes, spends and sometimes produces; and the external sector of trade with the rest of the world.
concepts.key_idea: Households, firms, government and the rest of the world are the four building blocks of macro analysis.
question_patterns: describe the four major sectors of an economy in the macroeconomic view
name the sectors into which macroeconomics divides the economy
what roles do households firms government and external sector play
how do the household and firm sectors depend on each other
which sector frames laws taxes and provides public services
explain why the rest of the world counts as a sector of the domestic economy

solution_steps.explain: Households supply labour and demand goods; firms hire inputs and produce output for sale.
Government frames and enforces laws, taxes, spends on infrastructure and services, and may itself produce.
Trade and capital flows with the rest of the world complete the four-sector picture.

concepts.title: Exports, Imports and External Trade
concepts.definition: Selling domestically produced goods to the rest of the world is exports, buying goods from abroad is imports, and alongside these flows capital can also move between the domestic economy and foreign countries.
concepts.key_idea: Exports bring foreign demand in, imports send domestic demand out, and capital may flow either way.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec101.txt, section 1.2, external sector paragraph, page 8
question_patterns: differentiate between exports and imports of a country
what kinds of trade connect a domestic economy with the rest of the world
when goods are sold abroad what are they called
explain how foreign capital flows affect the domestic economy
compute the trade balance from export and import values
why is the external sector important in macroeconomic study

solution_steps.action: Classify each flow as export or import
solution_steps.explain: Domestic goods sold abroad are exports; foreign goods bought by the home country are imports.

solution_steps.action: Take the difference of the two values
solution_steps.explain: Subtracting import value from export value gives the net trade balance with the rest of the world.

worked_examples.question_pattern: In an economy 12 million people are jobless and searching while 48 million are employed. Calculate the unemployment rate.

solution_template.explain: Employed plus jobless seekers gives 60 million.
12 of 60 is one fifth, so the rate is 20 percent.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A firm earns sales revenue of 900 and pays 200 as rent, 250 as interest and 300 as wages. Find the entrepreneur's profit.

solution_template.explain: Rent plus interest plus wages equals 750.
Revenue 900 minus 750 leaves a profit of 150.
